item.title: Ukraine Says It Received No Intelligence About Strikes 2 Nights in a Row
item.description:
Ukraine said it received no warning from its Western partners before a Russian missile attack against Kyiv on Tuesday night, after reporting earlier in the day that it had gotten no intelligence about a round of strikes the night before.

The news raised fears in Ukraine that the Trump administration had made good on apparent threats to cut off intelligence sharing that includes alerts of such attacks, even as both U.S. and Ukrainian officials asserted that intelligence continued to flow.

Before the latest Russian attack on Kyiv, President Trump said Tuesday that the United ⁠States was continuing to share intelligence with Ukraine. “We are helping them, and we are sharing intel,” he told reporters who had asked him about the possibility of cutting off intelligence if Kyiv did not halt strikes on Russian oil refineries.

The Ukrainian foreign minister also said on Tuesday that intelligence sharing was continuing, asserting that the attack the night before went undetected “because of a special type of weaponry which was used by the Russian side.”

Mr. Zelensky then weighed in again late on Tuesday, after the second ballistic missile attack. “Russian missile strike on Kyiv,” he wrote on social media. “Once again, no warning from our partners.”

He called the situation “absolutely unjust,” adding that Russia was “destroying our energy infrastructure, and Ukraine is not even receiving early warnings about ballistic missile launches.”

Commenting on the first attack, some military experts said there may have been no warning simply because it was not detected before launch, which has happened in the past, and not because of the United States withholding intelligence.

Russia has previously fired missiles that Western satellites have struggled to track, including S-400 missiles, which Ukraine has at times described as ballistic weapons. Serhiy Beskrestnov, a military expert who advises Mr. Zelensky, said after the attack on Monday that it was not the first time Western partners had failed to detect a launch of S-400 missiles.

Still, it would be unusual for Kyiv’s Western allies to fail to detect two missile attacks in a row.

Fears that Washington might cut off intelligence sharing with Ukraine emerged after Mr. Trump struck a deal with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia to buy millions of tons of Russian fuel. The agreement is part of an effort to bring down sky-high diesel prices, caused mostly by the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran, before the U.S. midterm elections.

As they presented the deal to the Ukrainians at a meeting last week in Miami, Trump administration officials asked Kyiv to stop striking Russian oil refineries so that Russian diesel could flow back onto the market. They said Kyiv owed Washington for critical U.S. intelligence assistance, which some in the room took as a veiled threat. A U.S. official later denied any suggestion that intelligence support would be withheld.

Mr. Zelensky said Ukraine had refrained from attacking Russian oil refineries over the past two days, framing it as a gesture of good will toward Mr. Trump, who on Friday declared an energy cease-fire that neither Kyiv nor Moscow has confirmed.

Ukraine has warned that such a cease-fire would work only if Russia stopped its attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities. Russia has continued to strike power plants even after Mr. Trump declared an energy cease-fire, Kyiv says. Mr. Zelensky said Tuesday night’s strike targeted a combined heat-and-power plant supplying Kyiv.

“The facts show that the Russians do not consider themselves bound by what the President of the United States said,” he wrote on social media. “Ukraine supported an energy cease-fire. Russia is targeting yet another power plant and the lives of our people.”

The Trump administration has shown before that it is willing to withhold intelligence as a lever against Ukraine. After a White House meeting in which Mr. Trump berated Mr. Zelensky in front of journalists in early 2025, Washington paused intelligence sharing with Ukraine for a few days.

On Monday, Russian missiles struck Kyiv around 10 p.m. local time. Air-raid alerts sounded too late, after the missiles had been launched, leaving residents with no warning. The lapse immediately prompted speculation online that Washington had halted intelligence sharing. Air-raid alerts sounded late, again, in the attack on Tuesday.

Ukraine lacks the extensive satellite-based intelligence capabilities of the United States and relies on information from Western partners to monitor Russian military preparations signaling an attack. That includes activity at air bases, movements of ships and the deployment of ballistic missile launchers.

“Our NATO partners inform us when there is activity involving strategic aviation. Flights from one airfield to another. Where missiles are being delivered,” Col. Yurii Ihnat, a Ukrainian Air Force spokesman, said in an interview this summer. Sometimes, he added, Western satellites detected a flash indicating a missile launch, and partners immediately informed Ukraine.

Commenting on the Monday attack, Colonel Ihnat told Ukrainian national television that Western intelligence sometimes “fails to arrive.”

“This is not the first case,” he said. “If there were certain technical issues this time, I believe the experts can sort it out. And we will resolve this problem together with our partners.”

Mr. Zelensky said Western intelligence was critical. “This is what helps prevent killings when there is a warning about ballistic missiles,” he said in a social media post on Tuesday.

The cost of missing early warnings is perhaps felt most keenly in the eastern Ukrainian city of Kharkiv, which lies only about 20 miles from the Russian border. Air-raid alerts sometimes cannot be sounded fast enough when Russia attacks the city.

On Monday night, volleys of drones hit Kharkiv, rocking the city center with loud, rumbling explosions. Fires burned in several locations. One strike tore into a residential building, collapsing apartments to the ground. The mayor, Ihor Terekhov, said in a social media post that four people had been killed on Monday and that two more strikes hit the city the next day.

On Tuesday, rescuers who worked through the night were still at the site of the residential building, pulling a body from the wreckage. Exhausted firefighters rested on the open trunks of vehicles as bulldozers cleared blackened rubble of bricks and belongings. A burning smell hung in the air.

Lyubov Smal, 69, one of the residents, with stitches on cuts to her face, said she had been cooking cutlets in her kitchen when a drone struck the building.

Bleeding, she made her way through smoke to the landing and was helped out by firefighters. Twelve hours later, she came back to plead for help in finding her cat. Resting from working through the night, two rescuers jumped up and climbed the blackened stairs to a third-floor apartment.

“He won’t bite us?” they jokingly asked. Minutes later, they were back with a big gray cat with yellow eyes. He dug his claws into the fleece of a neighbor, jumping at loud noises as bulldozers resumed clearing rubble.

Kamila Hrabchuk contributed reporting from Kharkiv.

item.title: U.K. and Europe Recoil From Trump’s Diesel Deal With Putin
item.description:
European and British officials were stunned by President Trump’s unexpected announcement that he had made a deal with President Vladimir V. Putin to purchase Russian diesel fuel. But they were in a bind on how to respond.

The arrangement, which President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine called “a gift” to President Putin, directly undercuts years of effort by dozens of countries — including the United States — to cut Russia off from the money that fuels Mr. Putin’s war of aggression in Ukraine.

Energy experts have said that the diesel agreement, if it goes ahead, could send some $4 billion of American money into the Russian economy.

Mr. Trump’s announcement on Friday afternoon of his “highly successful discussion” with Mr. Putin was all the more shocking in Europe as it came after Russia conducted several brutal strikes in Ukraine, killing 22 people including three babies in an apartment block on Wednesday and at least 30 people in a bus on Thursday.

For European leaders, the dilemma over the past three days has been familiar: How to support Ukraine in a moment of acute diplomatic peril, without triggering Mr. Trump’s ire?

As they scrambled for a response, they have stopped short of directly criticizing the American president and coalesced around a single diplomatic message: We are not changing our own approach to Russia, and we stand by Ukraine.

On Saturday, Britain announced that Prime Minister Andy Burnham had spoken to Mr. Zelensky, noting that he had begun the call “by recognizing the last 24 hours had been difficult for Ukraine” — an oblique reference to Mr. Trump’s intervention — and had “reiterated his complete solidarity.” The statement added that Mr. Burnham would meet with Mr. Zelensky in the coming days.

A spokesman for the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, told reporters that the government was “standing by the sanctions decisions against Russia and is working together with its European partners on further sanctions.”

Kaja Kallas, the European Union’s top diplomat, began her comments to reporters on Monday with a conciliatory nod to the United States, before saying that the bloc was “continuing our path” of trying to keep Russia from enriching itself by blocking the sale of oil and gas on the global market.

“The U.S. is our biggest ally, but our message is clear,” she said while entering a meeting of foreign affairs ministers in Luxembourg. “If we want to end this war, the only way we can do this is by putting more pressure on Russia.”

Margus Tsahkna, the minister of foreign affairs for Estonia, was more blunt.

“We have had this kind of turbulence and also pressure from President Trump’s side to Ukraine before,” he said. “So we need to focus on what we can do.”

Mr. Trump responded to the European reaction on his TruthSocial site Monday afternoon.

“The European Union paid Russia 250 Billion Dollars for Energy, and the Fake News Media doesn’t want to get near that story,” the president wrote, possibly referring to European purchases of Russian oil since Russia invaded. “I made the right choice for the American People — ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST!”

It is true that the European Union continues to buy Russian energy, though the bloc has been working to wean itself off it and has sharply reduced its dependence.

Since beginning his second term, Mr. Trump has repeatedly indicated support for Russia’s positions over those of Ukraine. Before his re-election, the president promised to end the war in 24 hours and has on several occasions blamed Mr. Zelensky for the continued fighting.

“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal, because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does,” Mr. Trump said Saturday.

On Sunday, the president announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an “ENERGY CEASEFIRE,” though neither side confirmed that such an agreement existed. Several European leaders on Monday welcomed such a cease-fire but noted that Russia struck Ukrainian energy facilities after the announcement.

For European officials, the latest example of the president’s go-it-alone diplomacy with Mr. Putin strikes at the heart of their attempts to maintain a consensus on opposing Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Nearly three dozen countries, including Britain, France and Germany, formed what they called the “coalition of the willing” last year to demonstrate their resolve in supporting Ukraine.

None of the countries want to engage in a direct military confrontation with Russia. Instead, they have focused on helping Ukraine acquire weapons to defend itself. And they have used economic sanctions designed to cut Russia off from its most lucrative exports.

On Monday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk of Poland urged the United States and other European nations to increase sanctions — not back away from them.

“This message must go out today from every capital, from Warsaw to Washington,” he said. “I am certain that our response in the coming hours, weeks and months will be one of full solidarity and determination on the part of the free world, all capitals and all political leaders.”

He added, in words that signaled a more complicated reality: “I very much hope so.”

item.title: Acclaimed Author Denies Using A.I. but Admits Plagiarism
item.description:
A Haitian-Canadian author accused of literary malpractice — including plagiarizing other writers and using artificial intelligence to write his award-winning new novel — has admitted to the plagiarism but denied using A.I. to write parts of the book.

The author, Thélyson Orélien, apologized in a statement on Tuesday for claiming “as my own texts that are not mine” — a reference to recent accusations that he had plagiarized the content of opinion articles and a short story that he published more than a decade ago.

But Mr. Orélien said that it was “slander and heresy” to claim that he had used A.I. to write parts of “It Was Either That or Die,” a novel published this year to initial acclaim.

“I did use research tools here and there, particularly when it came to foreign idioms,” Mr. Orélien said of writing that book, without clarifying what those tools were. “But no sentence in this book was created by a machine,” he added.

The accusations against Mr. Orélien last month turned into a literary scandal that rocked France and prompted deep soul-searching among the country’s writers and publishers about what the emergence of A.I. means for the future of literature.

It also led the jury of the Goncourt prize, France’s most prestigious literary award, to remove “It Was Either That or Die” from this year’s shortlist for the prize.

The furor erupted after a little-known social media account said it had run the book through an A.I.-detector tool called Pangram, which concluded it was written with the help of A.I. It was later revealed that the anonymous social media account was partly run by Samuel Fitoussi, a columnist at Le Figaro, a conservative daily newspaper.

In the immediate aftermath of those accusations, Mr. Orélien swiftly denied ever using A.I. to write his novel. But as the scandal grew bigger and accusations of plagiarism in his earlier writing surfaced, he refrained from commenting further on any of the accusations and put an abrupt end to his literary tour in France.

“Silence comes at a price: by staying silent, I was letting others tell my story for me,” the 38-year-old writer said on Tuesday, in a statement provided by his French publisher, railing against “experts” who “came after” his novel.

The author grew up in a middle-class family in Haiti and left for Canada after the 2010 earthquake that killed more than 200,000 people and destroyed his home. His novel, which depicts a migrant’s harrowing journey from Haiti to Canada, “comes from my own wounds and those of other migrants,” he said on Tuesday.

He started writing it in 2017, he said, and finished the first 300-page draft in 2019, years before A.I. tools were widely available. A.I. did not create “the meaning or structure of a narrative that comes from my gut,” he wrote on Tuesday.

He did, however, acknowledge plagiarism in earlier writing.

Radio Canada, Canada’s national public broadcaster, reported last month that Mr. Orélien had plagiarized four opinion articles published in 2012 and 2013 and that chunks of an award-winning 2012 short story, “Où va le monde,” resembled parts of a French book published in 1960, “Le Matin des Magiciens.”

On Tuesday Mr. Orélien listed a series of writers he said he admired at the time, including the authors of “Le Matin des Magiciens.”

“But admiration does not give me the right to take, to claim as my own, texts that are not mine,” he said.

“I made unacceptable mistakes, despite my youth and inexperience. I deeply regret this and present my apologies without reserve,” he added.

Mr. Orélien said that, though criticism was always legitimate, the “threats,” “media lynching” and “racist harassment” to which he had been subjected over the past few weeks had been “unbearable.”

He concluded by calling for his novel to be judged “for what it is.”

item.title: Russia Detains Japanese Journalist for Alleged Espionage
item.description:
Russia has detained a Japanese journalist for suspected espionage, the country’s main security agency said on Tuesday, alleging that the journalist had been collecting intelligence on the country’s military capabilities.

The agency, the Federal Security Service, said in a statement that the journalist, working for the Japanese newspaper Hokkaido Shimbun, was arrested in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, on the Pacific island of Sakhalin in Russia’s far east. It said the journalist, whom it did not name, had been transported to Moscow, where he was remanded into pretrial custody by the Lefortovo District Court.

“As a result of operational investigative measures, it was established that he was collecting and storing information related to the country’s defense capability, with the aim of transmitting it on instructions from national intelligence for use against the security of the Russian Federation,” the statement said.

The journalist was collecting data on the number of local recruits taking part in the war in Ukraine, the F.S.B. told the Russian news agency Tass.

The Japanese Embassy in Moscow and the country’s consulate in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk did not respond to a request for comment.

Maria Zakharova, a spokesperson for the Russian Foreign Ministry, identified the detained journalist as Yuki Imai.

“This incident will be an additional factor that darkens the atmosphere of Russian-Japanese relations,” Ms. Zakharova said in a statement.

Russian state-run television and news agencies broadcast a video of the journalist’s detention in what appeared to be a hotel room. The video showed papers marked “for internal use only.” With his face blurred, the journalist was shown being escorted to an airplane and then to a court building in Moscow. The video also showed a search being conducted in the newspaper’s bureau in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk.

Russia’s Foreign Ministry lists only one journalist accredited by the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, which is based on Hokkaido, a Japanese island just south of Sakhalin.

Russia has been engaged in a long-running territorial dispute with Japan over the Kuril Islands, which are controlled by Moscow but claimed by Tokyo as Japanese territory. Russia administers the Kurils from Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, as part of the Sakhalin region, but Japan, which calls them the Northern Territories, regards them as part of the Hokkaido prefecture.

The dispute intensified in August after President Vladimir V. Putin made his first ever visit to one of the islands, which was condemned by Japan.

The relationship between Russia and Japan was further challenged after Tokyo publicly said in July that Japan needed to improve its counterintelligence capacity. The announcement followed a report by The New York Times that revealed that Russian spies had been able to freely operate in the country, gathering intelligence and exporting goods that Moscow needs to prosecute its war in Ukraine.

At the beginning of October, speaking about the state of relations between the two countries Mr. Putin said that Russia was “interested in cooperation with Japan,” but he added that Moscow had been “concerned by Japan’s plans for militarization.”

In September, Mr. Putin said that “everything that is happening now, the deterioration in our relationship, is entirely down to the Japanese government.”

This is not the first time the F.S.B. has arrested a Japanese journalist on espionage accusations. In 2019, a Japanese journalist was detained in Vladivostok, a city in the far east of Russia, and accused of collecting classified information about the Russian military. At the time, no charges were pressed, and the journalist, who was not identified, was given three days to leave the country, Russian state news agencies reported.

In March 2023, a Wall Street Journal reporter, Evan Gershkovich, was arrested in the city of Yekaterinburg and accused of spying for America, which he and The Journal denied. He was sentenced to 16 years in prison before being released in August 2024 as part of the largest prisoner swap since the fall of the Soviet Union.

item.title: Saudi Energy Giant Struck as War Spikes Between Houthis and Saudi Arabia
item.description:
A building owned by the energy giant Aramco was set ablaze late Tuesday in a strike on the Saudi city housing its headquarters, the kingdom’s energy ministry said, as war spiked between the Houthi militia in Yemen and Saudi Arabia.

The Houthis had threatened earlier in the day to attack the Aramco headquarters in the eastern city of Dhahran, but did not immediately take responsibility for the strike. It came after the Iranian-backed militia reported that two major oil facilities in Yemen had been attacked by Saudi forces on Tuesday.

The Saudi energy ministry said in a statement that the strike in Dhahran had hit an Aramco administrative building and caused “a limited fire” and no injuries.

By late Tuesday, residents of both countries were on edge as explosions were repeatedly heard in their capital cities. A Saudi-led coalition said it was targeting Yemeni facilities that support the Houthi war effort, while the Houthis vowed to retaliate against comparable sites in Saudi Arabia.

The Saudi authorities issued warnings of an aerial threat in the Saudi capital, Riyadh. And Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki, a spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition, said four cruise missiles fired toward Riyadh and southern Saudi Arabia had been intercepted, along with two drones.

Mr. al-Maliki also reported that a ballistic missile launched toward the city of Damman in the eastern part of the kingdom by the Houthis had been intercepted, and that shrapnel fell in a residential area of neighboring Dhahran.

The Houthis have struck Aramco’s facilities before and have frequently hit Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea since tensions escalated between the two sides in July.

Yahya Saree, a military spokesman for the Houthis, had warned in a post on social media that, if Saudi forces were to attack Yemeni oil facilities, the militia would retaliate against Aramco’s headquarters, the company’s refinery in Riyadh and King Khalid International Airport, also in Riyadh.

The Houthis’ threat against Aramco came soon after Mr. al-Maliki urged civilians in Yemen to evacuate the vicinity of the al-Sabaha Central Station in Sanaa. Later on Tuesday, the Houthi-run television network al-Masirah reported that a Saudi airstrike had targeted that oil site.

Saudi strikes on the other oil facility, in port city of Hodeidah, killed at least two people, Anis al-Asbahi, a spokesman for the Houthi-run health ministry, said on Tuesday.

Shortly after the two oil facilities were reportedly struck, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen said it had targeted the Houthis’ military capabilities. In recent days, Houthi attacks have rocked Saudi Arabia, inflicting one of the highest death tolls there in years.

While the Saudis said they were “neutralizing the capabilities” of the militia, they did not confirm their targets. The coalition said in a statement that one oil complex in Sanaa, the Yemeni capital, and another in Hodeidah,were examples of civilian infrastructure that the Houthis were using to support their war effort.

Saudi warplanes have been bombing Houthi positions in Yemen in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government, which is fighting to retake territory seized by the Houthis last month.

Over the weekend, the Houthis carried out the deadliest attack on the kingdom in more than a decade, striking King Khalid International Airport and killing at least 13 people. More than 300 people were wounded in the Saturday attack, the Saudi authorities said.

On Tuesday, Saudi officials, during a cabinet meeting led by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, vowed that the Houthis would bear the consequences for the “heinous attacks” on the kingdom’s airport.

The Houthis on Sunday accused Saudi Arabia of bombing an airport in the Yemeni capital, according to statements carried by the Saba news agency, which is run by the militia. The Saudi authorities have not commented on that assertion.

President Trump, in a social media post after the exchange of threats on Tuesday, wrote that the “Houthis are behaving very badly.” He said that he thought the militia had “learned their lesson a year ago when we bombed the HELL out of them.”

Though Mr. Trump condemned the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia over the weekend, he has so far rebuffed the kingdom’s requests for U.S. support in the fight.

The Houthi militia has been fighting the internationally recognized, Saudi-backed government in Yemen since 2014. Saudi Arabia pledged to restore the government, declaring war on the Houthis and initiating a bombing campaign that set off one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. A fragile truce agreed to in 2022 has unraveled in recent months.

Emboldened by regional instability, the battle-hardened Houthis have far less to lose against their more powerful, wealthier enemies, even as they imperil Saudi Arabia’s ambitions to transform itself into a global hub of business and tourism.

The Red Cross called for the urgent de-escalation of the conflict on Tuesday, warning that further escalation would be disastrous for tens of millions of civilians. “Civilians are paying an unacceptable price as a result of military operations in the Middle East,” said Mirjana Spoljaric, the president of the International Committee of the Red Cross.

Shuaib Almosawa contributed reporting from Sanaa, Yemen.

item.title: Trump Hands Victories to Putin, Who Offers More War in Return
item.description:
The wins for President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia came in rapid succession from Washington.

President Trump proffered sanctions relief for Russian diesel fuel. He publicly called for Ukraine to get a new leader. And he pressured Kyiv to stop a strike campaign against Russian oil facilities that has damaged the Russian economy.

Mr. Putin, in return, offered more war.

Minutes after Mr. Trump announced the diesel deal, the Kremlin reiterated Mr. Putin’s stance that he would not negotiate with Ukraine at the moment, because he remained angry about Ukrainian strikes during last month’s Russian parliamentary election.

The next day, Russia launched an attack on the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia that killed 22 people, including four children. It was the latest in a near daily drumbeat of devastating Russian strikes, which have dramatically increased the civilian toll in Ukraine as Kyiv sorely lacks air-defense missiles.

And Mr. Putin has signaled that he plans to escalate further, aiming to knock out Ukraine’s power and water infrastructure in what Ukrainians expect to be the worst winter of the war.

Mr. Putin is reaping his victories as Mr. Trump’s own domestic political needs align with his longstanding inclination to tip the scales toward Russia. With the American president focused on trying to bring down fuel prices before a difficult midterm election, he is pushing Kyiv to trade away its leverage for nothing in return.

Ukraine has said it would suspend its oil refinery strikes if Russia ceased attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities heading into the winter. But when Mr. Trump announced an “energy cease-fire” on Sunday, he meant only a suspension of oil refinery strikes in both countries, The New York Times reported. Ukraine has only one major oil refinery, and Russian strikes took it largely out of service in 2022.

Mr. Trump has promoted his energy deal with Mr. Putin as an example of how he is tackling America’s diesel challenge, which experts say is more attributable to the war with Iran. But it was seen as a betrayal by Ukrainian officials, undercutting years of Western efforts to starve the Russian war machine of cash.

It may not even do much to lower diesel prices. Economists have said the amount of fuel discussed is not enough to move the needle significantly.

“The U.S. president is focused on one thing, which is himself and his reading of the world,” said Alexander Gabuev, director of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center.

That reading, Mr. Gabuev said, includes Mr. Trump’s stubborn denial that his own decision to go to war against Iran caused fuel prices to skyrocket. “In his picture of the world, the Gulf war doesn’t play a role in the current diesel crisis, and there needs to be a magical solution with someone he is predisposed to, who is Vladimir Putin.”

Earlier this year, things were looking difficult for Mr. Putin. Expenditures on the war were rapidly expanding. Progress on the battlefield had slowed to a crawl. Global prices for oil, Russia’s top export, had slumped to around $60 a barrel.

Then Mr. Trump launched the war in Iran, alongside Israel. Oil prices jumped to over $100 a barrel. The vast use of air defense missiles by the United States and its Gulf allies in response to Iran’s attacks dried up the supply for Ukraine, leaving it increasingly vulnerable. With Mr. Trump looking for a way out, Russia’s longstanding relationship with Iran offered Mr. Putin a new calling card with Washington.

As the Iran war accorded benefits to Russia, Ukraine tried to limit Moscow’s economic gains with increasingly effective strikes on oil refineries — the campaign that Mr. Trump is now demanding that Kyiv end.

Kyiv’s systematic targeting of Russian oil infrastructure brought the war home to Russia as never before, causing lines at the pump across the country and forcing Russia, one of the world’s largest diesel suppliers, to suspend exports.

As Ukrainian strikes decreased production, Russia’s tax revenue from oil and gas for the first three quarters of the year fell by 17 percent compared with the same period in 2025, even as fuel prices rose dramatically. (A rise in the ruble and Russian domestic fuel subsidies also played a role.)

Now, the diesel deal could pour billions of dollars into the Russian economy. An extended suspension of Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries, if Kyiv agrees to one under the intense American pressure, could generate much more money.

The wins for Mr. Putin go beyond the diesel deal. Mr. Trump has also welcomed Russian ministers this year for Group of 20 events in North Carolina and Wisconsin, and he plans to host Mr. Putin in December at the G-20 summit in Miami. His administration is also negotiating potential business deals with the Kremlin, in what Mr. Trump’s team has cast as inducements to a peace deal.

The Russians want even more from the U.S. president, analysts say.

When Mr. Trump returned to office in 2025, Moscow hoped that the United States would cut off all support for Ukraine and force President Volodymyr Zelensky into a capitulation largely on the Kremlin’s terms.

Mr. Trump’s Oval Office blowup with Mr. Zelensky in March of last year made it seem as if Moscow’s dream was within reach. The Trump administration’s decision to halt weapons donations to Ukraine and suspend intelligence sharing stoked hopes even further.

But in the months since, U.S. intelligence sharing resumed. Mr. Trump brokered a deal for the Europeans to buy weapons from the United States for Ukraine. And U.S.-led peace negotiations fizzled as the Trump administration became distracted by the war in Iran.

Fyodor Lukyanov, a Russian political scientist who advises the Kremlin, wrote last month that Ukraine would be left with little defense if the United States completely ceased its military support.

“But Trump is unlikely to take that step,” Mr. Lukyanov wrote, “even if he were personally inclined to do so,” because a complete Ukrainian defeat would not win him any plaudits in the American political establishment.

Such a move by Mr. Trump might also invite more aggressive actions from Congress, particularly after the midterms. The Senate recently passed a Russia sanctions bill, named in honor of Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina, with a veto-proof margin, though Mr. Trump retains the power to waive its provisions on national security grounds and will need to do so to import Russian diesel.

As Mr. Trump so far stops short of forcing Ukraine into a surrender, Mr. Putin is likely to continue his escalation, said Hanna Notte, an analyst at the James Martin Center for Nonproliferation Studies and the author of a new book on Russian foreign policy called “We Will Outlast Them.”

She said of Mr. Putin, “It’s quite clear that his intention right now is to inflict a really, really nasty winter on the Ukrainians.”

Although Russian forces remain largely stuck on the battlefield, Mr. Putin has long believed that he can achieve victory in Ukraine by outlasting Kyiv and what he sees as its fickle Western allies, analysts say. He believes they will eventually pull back their extensive support of Ukraine as their own domestic problems mount, analysts say.

The French presidential election next year could usher in the far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who has advocated halting financial assistance to Ukraine. Chancellor Friedrich Merz of Germany is also under pressure from a surging far-right party that has pressed for ending support for Ukraine. And both Britain and France are struggling under huge government debts that are far more expensive to service at current interest rates.

“You could make the case that from the Kremlin’s perspective, the future looks better, more conducive to an outcome of the war that is closer to their terms,” said Sam Charap, a Russia analyst at the RAND Corporation. “You have to change that perception of the future, diminish that optimism, to affect their calculus.”

item.title: The Oct. 7 Attack Changed Israel, but Not Its Politics
item.description:
For one day last week, much of Israel united to commemorate the anniversary of the deadliest attack in the country’s history.

But when Israelis head to the ballot box this month, they will be carrying sharply disparate versions of who is to blame for failing to prevent the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led assault. Though the attack traumatized Israel, it did not produce the kind of rage that would create a political transformation, leaving the country more polarized than ever.

The political divide is nowhere clearer than among the Israelis living closest to the Gaza border, where thousands of gunmen overran communities, army bases and a music festival.

In Nahal Oz, a pastoral kibbutz half a mile from the border, the gardens are blooming again with the return of residents evacuated during the war. Many in this liberal bastion are likely to vote against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his hawkish policies, holding him responsible for failures leading to Oct. 7, said Daniel Rahamim, 72, a spokesman for the community, who survived the assault along with his family.

“We don’t have the privilege of giving up on peace,” he said.

Barely eight miles away in the working-class town of Sderot, the scene of a fierce firefight during the Hamas-led attack, Mr. Netanyahu remains a hero. In the view of many residents, he was let down — or even betrayed — by his security chiefs in the run-up to Oct. 7 and on the day of the assault.

“If the left wins, we’re done for, it will be the end of Israel,” said Shlomi Aragon, 55, referring to anybody critical of Mr. Netanyahu.

The election, set for Oct. 27, will be the first since Hamas militants and their allies surged across the border from Gaza, killing about 1,200 people, mostly civilians, according to the Israeli authorities, and taking 251 hostages.

Israel’s devastating war in response reduced much of the Palestinian enclave to rubble and left more than 74,000 people dead, including thousands of children, according to Gaza health officials, who do not distinguish between civilians and combatants.

Many Israelis view this month’s vote as the most momentous since their country’s establishment nearly eight decades ago, and for reasons that are not limited to Oct. 7. Mr. Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition, Israel’s most hard-line and religiously conservative, has undermined the country’s democratic foundations, critics say, and left it diplomatically isolated.

Hanging over the election most intensely are questions about the missteps in the prelude to Oct. 7 — for the policies aimed at fostering quiet in Hamas-run Gaza in the years before the attack and for military and intelligence lapses that left Israel vulnerable. These failures have profoundly shaken people’s confidence in the state’s ability to protect them.

The wars that spread from Gaza to Lebanon and Iran in the aftermath of the Oct. 7 attack remain unfinished. Three years on, Israel’s enemies are battered but not out, defying Mr. Netanyahu’s promises of total victory.

Yet all this upheaval has not produced the radical shift that would upend Israel’s politics.

“Like everyone, after Oct. 7, I thought there would be an earthquake,” said Tamar Hermann, a professor of political science and expert in public opinion at the Israel Democracy Institute, a nonpartisan research group in Jerusalem.

Instead, she said, it has reinforced people’s previously held positions as they retreated to their political “comfort zones.”

Like past elections, this one, too, revolves largely around the question of “Yes Bibi or no Bibi,” Ms. Hermann said, using Mr. Netanyahu’s nickname, and the choice between a “more Jewish or more democratic” Israel.

The Netanyahu camp, for its part, says Israel’s security services failed to respond to the grave threat posed by Hamas, not the prime minister or the policies of his ruling Likud party.

There is little argument among most Israelis over the government’s new willingness to carry out sustained attacks beyond the country’s borders and occupy territory in Gaza, Syria and Lebanon. A majority of Israelis fear a repeat of Oct. 7, according to a recent survey by the Institute for National Security Studies at Tel Aviv University.

But that view does not extend to confidence in Mr. Netanyahu’s leadership. Surveys indicate a split electorate and a typically tight race with a high likelihood that neither Mr. Netanyahu, Israel’s longest serving prime minister, nor his chief rival, Gadi Eisenkot, a centrist and former military chief, will secure an easy path toward forming the next government.

On the Israeli side of the Gaza border, the air of renewal masks sharp disagreements over the lessons of Oct. 7.

During the attack, 15 people in Nahal Oz were killed, and eight residents were kidnapped, including one who died in captivity. Most of the residents have since returned to the kibbutz. At night, the lights of Israeli army positions visible along a ridge inside the Gaza Strip provide some sense of security.

Mr. Rahamim, the Nahal Oz spokesman, has a fresh tattoo on his arm bearing the date of the attack and the words, “On the path of hope.” The image of a sunflower climbing his forearm symbolizes a local crop — and hope, Mr. Rahamim said, “because it always faces the sun.”

In the last national election, held in 2022, 83 percent of the voters in Nahal Oz supported centrist and left-leaning parties. In the upcoming election, Mr. Rahamim said he and many neighbors will likely vote against Mr. Netanyahu again.

Mr. Netanyahu’s handling of Gaza is not the only reason. Mr. Rahamim also pointed to the government’s efforts at curbing the powers of the judiciary and at the influence Mr. Netanyahu’s ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies have over him, leading Mr. Rahamim to ask, “Will Israel be a liberal democratic state or gradually turn into a religious or fascist state?”

Some attitudes have hardened here, too, since the Oct. 7 attack. “If there is a consensus here in community, it is that Hamas has to be destroyed,” Mr. Rahamim said.

Unlike many in Mr. Netanyahu’s camp, Mr. Rahamim also said he believes that Israel must eventually negotiate an accommodation with moderate Palestinian leaders. “We have an obligation to our grandchildren,” he said.

In Sderot, forests of construction cranes rise from new neighborhoods. A serene memorial park has replaced the police station where a deadly battle raged. More than 50 people were killed in the city, including civilians, police officers, firefighters and soldiers.

Sderot has historically been a stronghold of Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party, and in the last election, 79 percent voted for the right-wing and strictly Orthodox parties that made up his governing coalition.

Here, residents espouse conspiracy theories spread by Mr. Netanyahu’s camp that treasonous generals and security chiefs kept the prime minister in the dark about the start of the Hamas attack.

Mr. Netanyahu has asserted that Israeli security officials had chosen not to awaken him in the early hours of Oct. 7, despite worrying signs from Gaza.. He has blocked the establishment of an independent inquiry into what went wrong, despite a strong public demand for one.

Mr. Aragon, who owns a shawarma restaurant, said he narrowly escaped death on Oct. 7 when gunmen drove behind him and started shooting. About 20 years ago, he said, his house was hit by a rocket from Gaza that severely injured his wife.

He described Mr. Netanyahu as “the war leader of a generation” and suggested that the Israeli air force, if activated, could have halted the Hamas invasion within an hour. “There was a betrayal. It’ll come out,” he said.

Living opposite the site of the destroyed police station, Evelyn Sayada, 60, whose son-in-law survived the assault on the music festival, said she felt constant anxiety because Hamas had not been disarmed. But she said she would almost certainly vote for Mr. Netanyahu, as her family has always done.

“I don’t think he failed,” she said. “There was treason.”

One of the worst-hit Israeli border villages was Kfar Aza, home to Yonatan Shamriz, 36. His brother, Alon, was taken hostage and later killed accidentally by Israeli soldiers in Gaza who had mistaken him and two other captives for militants.

Mr. Shamriz emerged from a life of relative obscurity and founded a grass-roots movement to cultivate new leadership and change called “Kumu!” — Hebrew for “awaken!” or “rise up!”

Faced with what they call government efforts to blur and forget, he and Kumu organized Israel’s main Oct. 7 memorial ceremony for the last three years, embracing families of victims from across Israeli society — left and right-wingers, religious and secular, Jews and Arabs. Tens of thousands attended this year’s memorial, and Israel’s leading television channels aired it live.

Mr. Shamriz now lives far from the Gaza border, in a trailer with his wife and three young children in a kibbutz on the coast north of Tel Aviv. He said he believes another attack like the one on Oct. 7 is a matter of time. “If not next year, then in 10 years,” he said.

Last year, Mr. Shamriz announced that he was entering politics, aiming to create a new, unifying force with a vision based on the lessons of Oct. 7. “Something young and fresh,” he said.

In September, he quit, concluding that Israelis weren’t ready to leave their old politics behind.

“For now, people are afraid of change,” he said. “Everyone wants to vote for an experienced politician or general — someone they know.”

item.title: A Father’s Mission Is to Show the World ‘What Russia Did to My Family’
item.description:
The 500-pound Russian bomb first appeared as a tiny blip on Yevhen Ovcharov’s live military map: a red speck gliding over the Ukrainian border and above the villages beyond.

Then he saw it hurtling toward his hometown, Sumy.

Yevhen was a Ukrainian soldier deployed 300 miles from home, on the eastern front. It was 9:45 p.m. on July 3 when he reached for his phone.

His wife, Nataliia Ovcharova, answered quickly. Don’t worry, she told him. She and the girls were fine and happily walking home from the park. Their 13-year-old, Veronika, was trailing slightly behind with a friend. Their youngest, Milana, who was 5, was beside her.

At 9:46, the call was cut off.

Yevhen called back once, twice, three times.

For six minutes, he heard nothing.

At 9:52, his phone rang. It was Veronika. She screamed that she was covered in blood. Milana, she said, was lying completely still on the ground.

“No one is helping,” she sobbed. “Dad, please come save us.”

Yevhen ran outside and jumped in a car to start the four-hour drive home.

This summer was Ukraine’s deadliest and most violent period since the first weeks of Russia’s invasion in 2022. Russian attacks killed more than 1,100 Ukrainian civilians from June to August, according to an estimate by the United Nations. Another 7,000 were wounded.

Russia preyed on Ukraine’s air-defense shortages, bombarding cities far from the front line with waves of drones and ballistic missiles that it knew Ukraine could not intercept.

Yevhen had been sent to fight in the eastern region of Donetsk, but his hometown in Ukraine’s northeast was the center of another Russian military push. Russia terrorized residential areas there with drones and glide bombs that it produces in large quantities.

Glide bombs have leveled cities across the country’s eastern and southern regions for years. The only way to stop these World War II-era weapons is with planes that shoot Russia’s fighter jets down before they drop the bombs. Ukraine still does not have the means to do that.In July, Russia launched a record 8,300 glide bombs. And at 9:46 p.m. on July 3, one landed in Sumy.

Veronika was 8 years old when the war started: old enough to understand that everything was changing but young enough that her parents still protected her from what they could.

Still, she could see how much her mom worried about her dad, a career police officer who was fighting in the infantry. Nataliia often asked Veronika to pray for him. As the oldest daughter, she told her, she had a special bond with her father. This was an important responsibility for Veronika, who often felt left behind by the attention on her sister, who was just a baby when Russia invaded.

“She was stressing a lot,” Veronika said of her mother. “When Dad was not reachable on the phone, she was panicking.”

Veronika didn’t worry like that. She got used to the explosions and the hum of Russian drones and the years that passed without her dad, who kept deploying to different parts of the front line.

When he had time off, Yevhen would come home and walk with her and Milana to the park for ice cream. Once, he arrived with a kitten he had found, a striped male with folded ears, whom he had named Max. The girls fell in love.

Veronika was growing up fast and took care of Milana while their dad was away and their mom expanded her beauty business, using the third bedroom that would one day be Milana’s to style women’s eyebrows and lashes.

The more time the sisters spent together, the less their age difference seemed to matter. “I could still talk to her about anything,” Veronika said. Milana was small but fiercely protective of Veronika. Once, she even threw a phone charger at a boy she saw bullying her sister. Veronika felt proud.

In May, Veronika turned 13. War or no war, she was thrilled by the idea of her first teenage summer: the freedom to roam the neighborhood with her large friend group. Her dad’s scheduled time off in July. The photo shoot her mom had booked for when they would all be together again. The trip they planned to a water park three hours away.

It would be Milana’s first time going anywhere. The girls couldn’t wait.

Yevhen got into the passenger seat of his friend’s car. While one friend drove, another, in the back, told him to hold on despite his panic.

Yevhen called everyone he knew in Sumy as they drove. The story about his family’s whereabouts kept changing. They were here, they were there.

It was past 2 a.m. when he arrived at the hospital. He rushed to the front desk and asked for the mother and daughter brought in a few hours before. The receptionist told him they weren’t there.

He ran outside and saw an ambulance.

“What happened to the woman and child who were wounded tonight?” he asked.

“They died,” the driver replied.

Veronika cut through the woods, slipped through a fence and walked down the bank of the shallow river until she reached a large rock. It was gray and smooth, with a curve that made it feel almost like a chair.

It had been two months since her mother and sister died, and she was 600 miles from home, the farthest she’d ever been. The sky was bright, and the mountains stretched into the sky.

The police had sent her and her father to this property nestled in the Carpathian Mountains a few weeks earlier. It was where Ukrainian police families like hers — with relatives who were wounded, dead or in need of a rest — could start to recover. There were no air-raid sirens, no explosions, no threatening hums from drones.

Veronika found the spot in the river on her own, when she wandered away from the wood-paneled building and the psychologist who kept asking how she felt. Away from the gym where her dad was always working out to manage his grief, and the pile of stuffed animals they had brought from home that reminded her of her sister. She returned to it nearly every day.

Veronika couldn’t think too much about her sister. When she did, her vision blurred, her heart pounded. She felt sick. She had learned that this is what doctors called a panic attack. She’d had three since that night in July.

The days passed slowly. She had visited the tourist markets and waterfalls and even climbed the tallest mountain in Ukraine, where visitors left messages for friends and relatives killed in the war.

But she was lonely and bored now. She wanted to go home.

She returned to scrolling on her new iPhone, the one she secretly wished for on this trip and that her dad bought her the very same day. She clocked 18 hours of screen time on it in a single day, most of it on TikTok. She tucked an AirPod into her right ear. She didn’t bother with the left ear: She hadn’t been able to hear out of it since the blast.

There was a necklace in her pocket, one that her mother had given her on her 13th birthday in May. She had not taken it off until the week before when a boy at the retreat pulled the chain and snapped it. She still wanted to keep it close to her as she waited for it to be fixed. The charm was thick and round and had words engraved along the edges.

“Dream, Act, Love. Daughter, you can do everything. I’m proud. I love you — Mom.”

While Veronika would sneak away to the river, Yevhen split his time between the gym and the psychologist’s office on the third floor. He made protein shakes to regain some of the strength he had lost to grief. He insisted sometimes on dragging Veronika away from her phone and taking her for hikes.

He didn’t want to sit still. When he sat for too long, he remembered too much, and ugly thoughts surged to the front of his mind. The thoughts told him that there was no point in living, that there would be no justice for his family.

The psychologist was helping him learn to push these thoughts away. To make plans instead. He was only 38. He knew he had to forge a path forward.

The first days after the deaths had been a blur of rage and stress. Yevhen broke the news to Veronika at the hospital and then slept by her bedside. Her legs and arm were pocked with bits of Russian shrapnel that later would cover her in purple scars. Her left ear drum had exploded from the shock wave.

At home, he took a blue Stitch stuffed animal that Milana had loved and stuck it in his bag. He decided to carry it with him everywhere.

He also searched for the police officer he heard had tried to save Milana. He wanted to ask him: Did you really do everything you could?

They met at the scene of the strike. The officer, Dmytro Zuienko, told Yevhen that he had been on a patrol and rushed there just after the explosion. He and a colleague performed CPR on Milana for 15 minutes, even after others moved away, afraid that another strike might be coming. Milana’s face, he told Yevhen, was stuck in his mind for days.

The officer went home that night, he said, his clothes soaked in blood, and told his wife that a girl had died in his arms who was only a few years younger than their own daughter.

Yevhen knew the officer was telling the truth. But he couldn’t forget the words Veronika screamed that night: “No one is helping.” If he had been there, would he have gotten to Milana faster than the officer? He couldn’t stop himself from asking that question again and again.

A few days later, Yevhen walked again to the spot where Natalia and Milana had been killed. He had dreams of transforming this road into an alley that would honor children killed in the war. But on this day, he planned only to leave candles at the makeshift memorial that neighbors and friends had built.

The sidewalk was covered with impact marks. The windows on the grocery behind were still boarded up. Flowers and stuffed animals adorned a broken tree.

When Yevhen looked up, Mykhailo Fedorov, the defense minister at the time, was walking toward him. Mr. Fedorov was in Sumy on that July day and had asked to visit the place where he heard a Russian glide bomb recently killed a mother and child.

Neither knew the other would be there.

Yevhen introduced himself, and the two men embraced. Yevhen’s story devastated Mr. Fedorov, who also had a young daughter. Both saw the chance meeting as an opportunity: Maybe Yevhen’s new mission could be to tell the world what happened to his family, to show everyone why Ukraine needed more air-defense systems, more planes. Maybe Yevhen could stop this tragedy from happening to anyone else.

They exchanged numbers. Later, at the police retreat, Yevhen thought about this idea constantly. It motivated him to stay alive.

Yevhen and Veronika left the mountains overnight on Sept. 14 and drove through winding roads in darkness. By morning they were in Kyiv, standing outside the children’s hospital where Aliona, one of the friends Veronika was walking with on July 3, was still a patient.

Aliona was 16. Russian shrapnel had maimed her legs. She’d already had 20 surgeries, and more were planned. Her doctors said she might never walk normally again.

Veronika burst through the door. She and Aliona held each other. Yevhen hugged Aliona’s mother, Iryna. They were old friends who shared another heavy grief: Iryna’s husband had died from cancer while Yevhen was on the front line.

“I missed you,” Aliona whispered to Veronika. “I want to go home.”

The girls compared scars. Veronika gave Aliona a teddy bear she had chosen from the mountain market and showed her the necklace the boy broke. Aliona tried to fix it. “I loved your mom,” she said when she read the charm’s message. She took a deep breath and covered her face with her hands.

The conversation turned back to the night of July 3.

Iryna was the first one there after the attack, she told Yevhen. She ran through dust and debris and found two men tying tourniquets around Aliona’s legs. She was sure her daughter was dead. She screamed. And then Aliona blinked. And when Iryna looked up, Veronika was standing there watching, her legs bloody, her face confused.

Veronika interjected to remind Iryna about her jean shorts. “They were bloody halfway up, if not more,” she said. “My sneakers were completely covered in blood, and my socks were covered in blood, too.”

“Veronika — imagine — she gets up and sees all of this. Everyone and everything,” Iryna said. “Aliona was lying facing upward, so she didn’t see it.”

As her mother talked, Aliona started to cry. Veronika did, too.In the next bed over, another teenage girl, wounded in a different strike on Sumy, sat and listened silently.

That afternoon, after Mr. Fedorov stopped by the hospital in Kyiv to visit Yevhen and the girls, and after a doctor checked Veronika’s ear and made plans for a future surgery, Yevhen and Veronika started the drive back to Sumy.

Yevhen’s mind was racing with plans. Mr. Fedorov, who had been fired in July but remained deeply involved in defense issues, suggested that morning that Yevhen should speak to officials in Sweden.

The Swedish government had promised jets to Ukraine to help shoot down planes before they could launch glide bombs, he said. Maybe Yevhen’s story could drive home the urgency and help the planes arrive sooner.

Yevhen agreed. It would the first step in his mission.

In Sumy, he and his daughter returned to an apartment that was too quiet and still. A pile of toys lined the back of the couch. Milana’s dollhouse sat nearby on the floor.

In Yevhen and Nataliia’s room, Milana’s bed was still pushed up against her parents’, the word “Princess” printed on its footboard. Yevhen took Stitch out of his bag and placed it on Milana’s pillow.

Veronika ran outside. She hadn’t told her friends when she would be back, and she decided to surprise them.

She hid behind a car, one hand on her mouth to muffle her giggles. She tilted her head to listen with her good ear and caught the sound of a faraway hum. “Is that an F.P.V.?” she asked. Satisfied it was not a Russian drone, she settled back into position.

Then she saw a group coming. She jumped out from her hiding place and onto her best friend, Uliana.

Just like that, Veronika was 13 again. She pulled a stuffed sheep she had bought in the mountains from her pink backpack and shoved it into Uliana’s hands. She showed off the new pink shorts and Nike sneakers her dad had bought her in Kyiv and held out her new iPhone. Her friends looked at her things with a hint of envy. No one talked about why she had been gone.At home, Yevhen retreated to the room where he had arranged a shrine to his wife and younger daughter. He lit candles, touched their photos and bowed his head in prayer.In the room next door, Veronika and Uliana were now planning a sleepover. They squealed and giggled and ignored the Russian drones packed with explosives that buzzed just outside their window.

The next day, Yevhen stood in the cemetery, tidying Milana and Nataliia’s graves.

So many toys were piled up from visitors paying their respects that some had started to fall to the ground. “Daughter, Daddy loves you,” he whispered. “He doesn’t forget about you.”An explosion shook the city. “They probably hit the checkpoint behind us,” Yevhen said, barely looking up. He touched the signs above the graves with his wife’s and daughter’s names and then, crying, kissed them. He thought again about his new mission.

“Let the world see what Russia did to my family,” he said as he walked to the car. “I want to tell Europe and the United States that our kids also want to live.”He looked back at his wife’s and daughter’s graves. “They also wanted to live.”

On Sept. 21, Yevhen and Veronika drove west again, back to Kyiv.

They boarded a morning train to Budapest, where they spent one night before they caught a flight to Stockholm. Mr. Fedorov had arranged the trip, and a Ukrainian businessman, Oleh Horokhovskyi, paid for it.

The Swedish defense minister had agreed to meet them. They were going to describe to him what happened to their family.They knew that sharing their story would not change its ending. They wanted to tell it anyway.

Thank you so much for reading this article about Yevhen and Veronika. I first heard of them in July, when I saw that a girl lost her mother and younger sister in Sumy. I wanted to follow what grief looked like for a teenager still living through the war. Then I learned her father was a soldier. My colleagues and I spent a lot of time with Yevhen and Veronika, watching them navigate the aftermath of this tragedy. We were profoundly affected by their love for each other and desire to protect each other from their own versions of grief. We also saw how Yevhen sought a mission and Veronika sought some return to a sense of normalcy, and how those two realities somehow clashed. I’m happy to answer any questions about our reporting process and about the family. They both were very open with us and grateful to share their story and worlds with us, which made this story even more intimate.

Nataliia Novosolova contributed reporting from Kyiv.
